source_facts: Trellis 5.1 is a synthetic event service. This specification is authoritative for its consumer contract. Event transport is at-least-once while an unacknowledged event remains within retention. No numeric retention period is specified. The JSON event identifier field is event_key; its value identifies a logical event and remains stable across deliveries of that event. The JSON delivery-attempt identifier field is receipt_key; its value identifies one delivery attempt and changes on redelivery. Consumers MUST acknowledge using the receipt_key of the delivery being acknowledged. Consumers MUST NOT acknowledge before the local business transaction commits. With a retained event_key deduplication record, committing that record and the business update in one database transaction provides exactly-once committed effects in that database. The deduplication record is uniquely keyed by event_key, and the atomic transaction permits a business update only when inserting a previously absent event record. Committing the same two writes in separate transactions, with the business update committed first and the deduplication record committed second, provides only at-least-once committed-effect behavior under retries. These two cases assume the same stable event identifier and must be distinguished by transaction placement. Neither case makes handler invocation exactly-once. External HTTP side effects are outside the database guarantee. Consumers MUST retain deduplication records while the corresponding events remain replayable. Consumers SHOULD acknowledge within 30 seconds after commit; this is an operational recommendation, not a protocol validity deadline. Consumers MUST use an acknowledgment body of at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes; exactly 4096 bytes are accepted by this size rule and 4097 bytes are rejected. Receipt age is measured in seconds from issuance using the service clock. An acknowledgment is valid with respect to receipt age only while age is strictly less than 300 seconds; a receipt exactly 300 seconds old is expired. Size acceptance does not override receipt expiry, and receipt-age validity does not override the body-size cap. The valid-receipt acknowledgment request is POST /v1/acks with JSON body {"receipt_key":"r_82"}, using the current receipt value. The illustrative event is {"event_key":"e_14","receipt_key":"r_82"}; its redelivery may have receipt_key r_83 with event_key e_14. A handler for an already committed event should use the existing deduplication record to avoid another business update and acknowledge the current delivery. These examples specify identity and transaction behavior without prescribing authentication, a database engine, retry delays, or a wire error code.

# Trellis 5.1 consumer integration

This guide describes the event identities, local transaction boundary, and acknowledgment rules used by a Trellis consumer. Use it when connecting an application handler to a database-backed business operation. The transport contract and the database-effect contract describe different parts of that integration. Keep both in view when deciding what a completed handler means for the application. In practical terms, there is more than one kind of completion involved in this workflow, and those kinds of completion relate to different parts of the workflow.

## Read the two identities

The logical event identifier is the JSON field `event_key`. Its value remains the same when Trellis delivers the same logical event again. The delivery-attempt identifier is the JSON field `receipt_key`. Its value identifies one attempt and changes on redelivery. These two fields can appear next to each other in a payload, but they answer different questions about the event being handled.

For example, an initial delivery can contain:

```json
{"event_key":"e_14","receipt_key":"r_82"}
```

A later delivery of that same event can still carry `event_key` equal to `e_14` while carrying `receipt_key` equal to `r_83`. The logical work is the same work; the acknowledgment identity belongs to the later attempt. Use the event identifier when recording that business work has already committed. Use the receipt identifier when acknowledging the particular delivery in hand. Do not infer that a changed receipt means a new business event.

## Understand what can repeat

Trellis transport is at-least-once while an unacknowledged event remains within retention. A handler may therefore encounter an event it has already seen. The database technique below concerns committed business effects rather than the number of times code enters the handler. Neither transaction arrangement described here promises exactly-once handler invocation.

Consider the event identity before performing another business update. If a retained deduplication record shows that the event already committed, use that record to avoid another business update and acknowledge the current delivery. The relevant record is keyed by the logical event, even though the acknowledgment will use a delivery-attempt identifier. This distinction allows an application to recognize the same work without treating the older receipt as the acknowledgment token for a newer attempt.

## Place the deduplication record

With a retained `event_key` deduplication record, committing the record and the business update in one database transaction gives exactly-once committed effects in that database. The record is uniquely keyed by `event_key`; the atomic transaction permits a business update only when inserting a previously absent event record. The guarantee applies to the committed database effects associated with the event. It does not claim that every execution of the handler is unique.

With a retained `event_key` deduplication record, committing the record and the business update in separate database transactions also gives exactly-once committed effects in that database. In this arrangement, the business update commits first, and the deduplication record commits second. The record is still keyed by the stable logical event identifier. The practical distinction to consider is where the two writes commit relative to each other, rather than whether the receipt identifier happens to remain available in application memory.

An external HTTP side effect is outside the database guarantee. A request sent to another service is not included merely because the handler also writes a deduplication record locally. When describing the integration to another application team, specify which committed effects are in the database transaction. A statement about database effects should not be presented as a statement about all effects the handler might initiate.

Consumers MUST retain deduplication records while the corresponding events remain replayable. The retention condition follows the replayability of the events; it is not expressed here as a fixed number of hours or days. The record is what lets the handler recognize already committed logical work when a replay occurs.

## Acknowledge after commit

Consumers MUST NOT acknowledge before the local business transaction commits. Treat this as an ordering rule for the business operation and its acknowledgment. Consumers MUST acknowledge using the `receipt_key` of the delivery being acknowledged. For the first example delivery, the request is `POST /v1/acks` with this body:

```json
{"receipt_key":"r_82"}
```

If the delivery in hand instead carries `r_83`, use that current receipt value. Do not substitute `event_key` for the receipt field because the event identifier was used for database deduplication. The identifier used to recognize committed work and the identifier used to acknowledge a delivery have separate roles.

Consumers MUST acknowledge within 30 seconds after commit. This timing statement concerns the interval after the local transaction has committed. It is separate from the age limit of the receipt itself, which is measured from issuance and is described below. Do not calculate receipt age by starting a new clock when the database commit completes.

## Apply the size and age rules

Consumers MUST use an acknowledgment body of at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes. Exactly 4096 bytes are accepted by this size rule; 4097 bytes are rejected. This limit measures encoded bytes in the body, not the number of visible characters in an editor. The example body above illustrates the field, rather than a requirement to pad a body to the allowed maximum.

Receipt age is measured in seconds from issuance using the service clock. An acknowledgment is valid with respect to age only while the receipt is strictly less than 300 seconds old. At exactly 300 seconds, the receipt is expired. The size rule includes equality at its upper limit, while the receipt-age rule excludes equality at its upper limit. Keep those comparisons attached to their own quantities when implementing the consumer.

The two checks answer independent questions. A body that meets the byte limit does not make an expired receipt valid. A receipt that meets the age limit does not allow an oversized body. Apply each rule to its own input rather than treating either check as general acknowledgment approval.

requirements.description: Preserve event_key as the exact logical-event identifier field name.
The logical-event identifier remains stable across redeliveries of one event.
Preserve receipt_key as the exact delivery-attempt identifier field name.
The delivery-attempt identifier changes on redelivery.
Acknowledgment MUST use the receipt identifier of the delivery being acknowledged.
Acknowledgment MUST NOT precede the local business transaction commit.
Retaining a uniquely event-keyed deduplication record and atomically gating the business update on inserting that absent record provides exactly-once committed effects in the database.
With a retained event deduplication record, committing the business update before a separate deduplication-record commit provides only at-least-once committed-effect behavior under retries.
Event transport is at-least-once while an unacknowledged event remains within retention.
Exactly-once handler invocation is not guaranteed.
External HTTP side effects are outside the database guarantee.
Deduplication records MUST remain retained while the corresponding events are replayable.
Acknowledging within 30 seconds after commit is a SHOULD recommendation rather than a MUST deadline.
An acknowledgment body of exactly 4096 UTF-8 bytes is accepted by the size rule.
An acknowledgment body exceeding 4096 UTF-8 bytes is rejected by the size rule.
Receipt age is measured in seconds from issuance on the service clock.
Receipt-age validity requires age strictly less than 300 seconds.
A handler recognizing an already committed event from its retained deduplication record avoids repeating the business update.

issues.description: The separate-transactions paragraph claims exactly-once database effects, incorrectly extending the atomic-transaction guarantee to separate commits.
issues.acceptable_resolution: State that separate commits provide only at-least-once committed-effect behavior under retries. Preserve the exactly-once database guarantee for the atomic case and keep both otherwise similar conditions distinguishable.

issues.description: The after-commit timing paragraph promotes the 30-second acknowledgment recommendation from SHOULD to MUST.
issues.acceptable_resolution: Restore SHOULD for acknowledgment within 30 seconds after commit and explain that it is not a protocol validity deadline. Retain the independent mandatory ordering rule and strict receipt-age limit.
